how-to-price-music-lessons.html.text:
← Music lesson pricing calculator

How to price music lessons without guessing

A published rate of $60 an hour does not mean you are paid $60 for every hour you spend teaching. Preparation, travel, and cancellations all consume calendar time that a flat hourly rate hides. Pricing from your real teaching week — not the 60 minutes in front of a student — is what tells you whether your rate actually supports your target income.

Open the free lesson pricing calculator

What a per-hour rate does not show

Cancellations and no-shows. A scheduled lesson that cancels still held the slot. At a 10% cancellation rate, 960 scheduled lessons a year pay for only 864 of them — the other 96 are calendar time with no revenue.

Preparation and travel minutes. Ten minutes of prep per lesson turns a 960-lesson year into 1,120 hours of work, not 960. Travel adds further hours without adding a dollar at the same price, which is why it moves your effective hourly rate but not your annual cash.

Fixed studio costs. Rent, materials, and software subscriptions have to be paid whether or not a lesson happens, so they belong in the price per paid lesson, not treated as a rounding error.

Worked example

20 lessons scheduled per week, 48 teaching weeks a year, a 10% cancellation rate, 10 minutes of prep per lesson, no travel, $200 in monthly studio costs, and a $40,000 target annual pay after costs:

FigureValue
Paid lessons per year864 of 960 scheduled
Annual hours (including prep)1,120
Break-even price$2.78 per lesson
Price that hits the $40,000 target$49.07 per lesson
Effective hourly at a $60 price$44.14

Two levers change that $49.07 target price without raising your published rate: cutting cancellations by 5 points brings it down to $46.49, and adding two more weekly lessons brings it down to $44.61 by spreading the same fixed costs over more paid lessons. Thirty minutes of travel per lesson changes neither number — it only drops the effective hourly rate from $44.14 to $30.90 for the same cash.

Common questions

How much should I charge for private music lessons?

Start from your target annual pay after costs, not a rate you have seen a nearby teacher charge. Divide your target pay plus your annual studio costs by the number of lessons you actually expect to be paid for once cancellations are subtracted — not the number you schedule. For 20 lessons a week, 48 weeks a year, a 10% cancellation rate, and $200 in monthly costs against a $40,000 target, that price is $49.07, not $40,000 divided by 960 scheduled lessons.

Does a cancellation policy actually change my hourly rate?

Yes, because an empty slot still cost you the calendar time even though it paid nothing. Tightening cancellations from 10% to 5% on the same schedule raises paid lessons and annual revenue without changing your published price, which lowers the price you would otherwise need to charge to hit the same target — in the worked example below, the target price drops from $49.07 to $46.49.

Should I charge more for lessons that require travel?

Travel time changes your effective hourly rate, not the cash a lesson brings in at a given price. Thirty minutes of travel per lesson does not move annual revenue or net income at all — it only stretches the same income across more hours, which is why a house-call rate is usually justified by the added hours, not by the drive itself.

Why the number changes

A 60-minute lesson can consume preparation, driving, setup, and an empty slot after a cancellation. This calculator makes those invisible hours visible so you can decide whether to raise the rate, tighten your cancellation policy, or teach fewer locations.

Search questions answered: how much should I charge for music lessons, how to price private piano lessons, and what is my real hourly rate as a music teacher? See the full pricing guide with a worked example, how this compares to a studio-management platform like My Music Staff, or what copying the going local rate misses about your own week.

Common questions

Why is the break-even price so much lower than what I actually charge?

Because break-even only has to cover your fixed monthly costs, spread across every paid lesson — it says nothing about your own pay. At the defaults, $200/month in costs is $2,400/year against 864 paid lessons, a break-even price of just $2.78. The gap between that and your $60 rate is what pays you, not what pays your studio bills.

Why is my effective hourly lower than my lesson price?

Because a lesson slot is never really 60 minutes of paid work. At the defaults, 10 minutes of prep and 0 minutes of travel make each scheduled slot 70 minutes, so $60 earned across 70 minutes of real time works out to an effective hourly of about $44.14 — not $60. Add travel and the gap grows further, since travel time is unpaid time attached to a paid lesson.

What does the cancellation rate actually cost me?

At the default 10% cancellation rate, 960 scheduled lessons a year become 864 paid ones — 96 empty slots you still had to hold time open for but never got paid to fill. Tightening that rate is one of the two levers the comparison table checks, because it recovers lessons you already scheduled rather than requiring you to find new students.

Does adding travel change my income?

No. Travel time changes your effective hourly rate, not your cash: the comparison table's note holds because annual revenue only depends on paid lessons and price, and travel minutes never enter that calculation. What travel does is stretch the hours you spend earning that same revenue, which is why the effective-hourly column moves and the net-after-costs column does not.

Which change is worth more: fewer cancellations or two more weekly lessons?

It depends on your numbers, which is why the table compares both against your actual week rather than assuming one is always better. Five fewer points of cancellations recovers lessons you already scheduled; two more weekly lessons adds new scheduled time (and its own prep and travel) on top. Read the “Net after costs” column for whichever change moves more annual cash at your price and volume.

Is my rate and teaching schedule uploaded anywhere?

No. Every figure is calculated in your browser and saved only to this browser's local storage so the form remembers your numbers next visit — nothing is sent to a server, and no accounts or analytics vendors are involved. “Copy share link” encodes the same teaching-week fields into the page's own URL fragment (never sent to a server) so you can hand a live, editable scenario to another teacher, a bookkeeper, or a studio partner.

Privacy: Everything runs in your browser. Your inputs are never uploaded. We count only anonymous feature events in local storage, never people, IPs, or content. Clear storage or enable the browser's Do Not Track / Global Privacy Control signal to stop counting.

← Music Lesson Pricing Calculator

This calculator vs. My Music Staff

Two different jobs: My Music Staff is a paid subscription that runs a studio's scheduling, billing, and attendance. This page is a free, private calculator for one narrower question — what should the lesson price be, once cancellations, prep, travel, and monthly costs are counted — with nothing to sign up for.

What each tool is for

My Music Staff is a well-known paid subscription platform for independent music teachers and studios, built to run the operational side of teaching: online lesson scheduling, automated billing and payment collection, attendance and makeup-lesson tracking, and parent or student communication, described on its own site. It is the kind of tool a teacher reaches for once they already have a lesson price and need the calendar, invoices, and reminders built around a growing roster of students. My Music Staff's own pricing and plan terms are not repeated here, since this session cannot verify today's figures against its current terms; only its well-documented scope as a studio-management platform is described.

This calculator does none of what a studio-management platform does. It has no scheduling, no billing, no student roster, and no account. It takes the annual pay target, teaching weeks, cancellation rate, prep and travel minutes, and monthly costs a teacher already has in mind, and returns the lesson price needed to hit that target and the real effective hourly rate once the invisible time is counted — instantly, in the browser, with nothing uploaded and nothing to configure first.

QuestionWhere to answer it
What should I actually charge per lesson to hit my annual income target, once cancellations and unpaid prep time are counted?This calculator — free, instant, private, no account or student roster needed.
How do I schedule lessons, collect payment automatically, and track attendance across a growing roster of students?My Music Staff or a comparable studio platform — that ongoing operational workflow is what it is built for.
Is my quoted rate still worth it once driving time and an empty slot after a last-minute cancellation are counted?This calculator — travel and cancellation fields show the real effective hourly rate directly.
Do I need parent communication, online booking, or recurring invoice reminders for an existing studio?My Music Staff or a comparable platform — this page remembers nothing about students between visits except what your own browser stores locally.
Do I need an account, a student database, or a payment processor to use the tool?This calculator: no. My Music Staff's scheduling and billing run inside a configured, ongoing studio account.

Most independent teachers get different value from each: My Music Staff (or a comparable studio platform) for the ongoing scheduling, billing, and communication behind a running roster of students, and a private calculator like this one for setting the lesson price honestly before any of that billing starts. This page's own figures are a pricing worksheet, not a scheduler, a payment processor, or a substitute for the platform you actually run your studio in.

It answers the narrower question that comes first: from your annual pay target, real teaching weeks, cancellation rate, prep and travel time, and monthly costs, what should the lesson price actually be. Once you have that number, My Music Staff (or a comparable studio platform) is where you might run the calendar and invoicing around it.

vs-picking-a-rate-off-the-going-local-pr.text:
← Music Lesson Pricing Calculator

This calculator vs. picking a rate off the going local price

Matching what other teachers post nearby tells you the number is competitive. It says nothing about whether it covers your own cancellations, prep and travel time, studio costs, or the income you actually need — the arithmetic this calculator does instead.

What picking the going local rate is

Checking what nearby teachers or studios charge and matching it — or pricing a little under it — is the fastest way to set a rate. It needs no arithmetic, and it keeps a new teacher's price from looking out of line with the market they are entering.

What it cannot do is see the week behind that number. The going rate is an average (or a guess at one) across teachers with different cancellation rates, different amounts of drive time, different prep habits, and different income needs. Copying it assumes your week looks like theirs.

What this calculator is

This page keeps no account and sends nothing to a server. You enter your lesson price, scheduled lessons per week, teaching weeks per year, cancellation rate, prep and travel minutes per lesson, monthly costs, and target annual pay. It returns the break-even price, the price that reaches your target, your current annual revenue, and the effective hourly rate once prep, travel, and cancelled slots are counted — for your own week, not the going rate for lessons in general.

What the going local rate doesWhat this calculator does instead
Reflects what other teachers charge, which may or may not include their own travel time, cancellation rate, or costs. Takes your own travel minutes, cancellation rate, and monthly costs, and prices your week specifically.
Has no line for an income target, so it cannot say whether the number supports the pay you actually need. Compares your current price against the price that reaches your stated target annual pay.
Quotes a per-lesson price, not a per-hour one, so it hides how much of a scheduled slot is unpaid prep and travel time. Reports the effective hourly rate once prep and travel minutes are added to every scheduled lesson.
Does not account for lessons you are scheduled to teach but do not get paid for. Applies your cancellation rate to scheduled lessons before pricing, so the target and break-even figures are built on paid lessons, not scheduled ones.
Gives a single number to charge, not a number to check that price against. Reports break-even, target price, and effective hourly side by side, so a going rate can be scored against your own numbers before you adopt it.

One going rate, two very different weeks

Using this calculator's own figures: a teacher who checks nearby listings and settles on the going local rate of $50 a lesson, teaching 16 lessons a week for 44 weeks a year with a 15% cancellation rate, 10 minutes of prep and 25 minutes of travel per lesson (a house-call teacher), $120 a month in costs, and a $45,000 annual pay target, nets $28,480 a year across 1,114.7 real hours of scheduled, unpaid, and travel time — an effective hourly of just $25.55, and $16,520 short of the stated target. The price that actually reaches $45,000 under this same week is $77.61, not $50 — a $27.61-per-lesson gap the going rate never surfaces, because it was set by teachers whose weeks may carry none of this teacher's travel time or cancellation rate.

Common questions

What does picking a rate off the going local price actually tell you?

It tells you what nearby teachers or studios post, which is a starting point for staying competitive -- not a statement about whether that number covers your own cancellations, prep and travel time, studio costs, or income target. Two teachers charging the same $50 can be in very different positions: one drives nowhere and rarely gets cancelled on, the other spends 25 minutes traveling to every lesson and loses 15% of bookings to no-shows. The going rate cannot see either difference.

How big is the gap in practice?

Using this calculator's own figures: a teacher charging the going local rate of $50 a lesson, teaching 16 lessons a week for 44 weeks with 15% cancellations, 10 minutes of prep and 25 minutes of travel per lesson, and $120 a month in costs, nets $28,480 a year for 1,114.7 real hours of work -- an effective hourly of $25.55, and $16,520 short of a $45,000 target. The price that actually reaches that target is $77.61, not $50 -- a $27.61 gap the going rate never surfaces because it was never asked to.

Is charging the going local rate ever fine?

For a teacher whose cancellations, prep, travel, and costs happen to sit near what the going rate assumes -- often a studio teacher with no drive time and a stable roster -- the going rate can land close to a sustainable number, because it was probably set by teachers in a similar position. The risk is copying that number into a different week: adding travel, a higher no-show rate, or a specific income target changes the math the going rate never accounted for, and by the time a teacher notices the shortfall a year of lessons has already been taught at it.

Does this calculator know what other teachers in my area charge?

No. It has no data on your local market, competing studios, or what a going rate is in your city. It takes your own lesson price, schedule, cancellation rate, prep and travel time, monthly costs, and target pay, and returns the price, break-even, and effective hourly your own week produces -- the arithmetic a rate copied from someone else's listing skips, not a market survey.
